screens.title: Web and Database Services Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will study the essential steps to get a web server and a database server running and reachable on a RHEL system. We'll cover installing Apache HTTPD and MariaDB using the dnf package manager, starting and enabling services with systemctl, and the basic security steps that make these services safe to expose. You will see concrete commands to create a simple web page under the default document root, adjust SELinux contexts and file permissions when Apache cannot read files, and open HTTP and HTTPS through firewalld so external clients can reach your server. By the end of this chapter you will be able to install both services, verify they run, fix basic access problems, and perform the initial hardening steps that reduce risk. Consider how least privilege and routine updates fit into daily administration — that mindset makes these steps meaningful beyond the commands.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Lab Flow
screens.narratorSegment: This page outlines a recommended sequence so your lab runs without surprises. Start by installing packages with dnf so the binaries and unit files exist. Then enable and start services to ensure systemctl-created sockets and directories are present; this avoids file-permission anomalies later. Next, create a minimal index file in the default document root and adjust SELinux contexts and ownership so Apache can read it. Only after the service runs and file access is confirmed should you change firewall rules to expose the service. For MariaDB, install and start the service, then immediately run mysql_secure_installation to remove anonymous users and set root password. Test the database locally before permitting remote access. Following this order reduces troubleshooting complexity: if you open firewall ports before verifying service availability, you may think the firewall is the problem when the service itself is down or misconfigured. Practice the sequence in the lab to build muscle memory. The lab activity included in the chapter follows this flow step-by-step and ends with a verification step: browse to http://your_rhel_server_ip and log into MariaDB locally. Which step would you try twice to gain confidence?

screens.title: Installing Apache HTTPD
screens.narratorSegment: To install Apache HTTPD on RHEL you use the distribution package manager so the httpd binary, unit files, and configuration skeleton are all placed correctly. The canonical command is sudo dnf install -y httpd. Running this fetches the httpd package and any required dependencies. After installation, systemctl knows about the httpd unit and you can enable and start it with sudo systemctl enable --now httpd. Enabling with --now both starts the service immediately and ensures it will start on boot. Verify the unit with sudo systemctl status httpd which reports whether the service is active and any recent errors. A concrete example: in the lab you might install httpd, enable the service, then check status and see it active. If status shows a failure, examine the journal with sudo journalctl -u httpd. A common misconception is that package installation alone makes the site reachable; you must start and enable the service. Also avoid assuming the default document root contains your custom content — create an index page explicitly. Practice these commands until you can reliably install, start, and check httpd. What would you check first if systemctl status shows the service failed?

keyIdea.title: Install + enable
keyIdea.text: Use dnf to install httpd, then enable and start with systemctl so the web server runs now and after reboot.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Install Apache
Install with dnf and enable the httpd service
Commands you will run in the lab.
<sudo dnf install -y httpd>
<sudo systemctl enable --now httpd>
<sudo systemctl status httpd>
<sudo journalctl -u httpd --since '5 minutes ago'>
Note: enabling with --now saves a step. If status reports failure, check journalctl for configuration errors or missing dependencies before changing firewall rules.
Explanation & example
  • dnf installs packaged files to their standard locations so systemctl can manage the unit.
  • systemctl enable --now both starts the service now and enables it at boot, preventing service absence after a reboot.
  • Use journalctl to view recent unit logs if status shows failed; it reveals config errors or permission problems.
Example scenario
You install httpd, enable the service, then browse to the server IP and see nothing. Before opening firewall ports, confirm systemctl status shows active; if not, check journalctl -u httpd.
Key Takeaway

Installing a package is only the first step. Enable and start the service and check logs to ensure the server runs.

screens.title: Default Document Root and index.html
screens.narratorSegment: Apache serves files from a document root. On RHEL the default is /var/www/html. Creating a simple index. html file there is the fastest way to verify the server serves content. For example, echo "<h1>Welcome to my Cohortia RHEL Web Server!</h1>" | sudo tee /var/www/html/index. html writes a test page. After placing the file, ensure the httpd service is running and then browse to the server IP or curl the address locally. A common mistake is assuming the file is readable—permissions or SELinux contexts may prevent Apache from serving it. Use sudo chmod -R 755 /var/www/html and sudo chown -R apache:apache /var/www/html to set ownership and basic permissions. If SELinux prevents access, restore contexts with sudo restorecon -Rv /var/www/html. Another misconception is that the index filename can be arbitrary; by default Apache looks for index. html among other welcome files, so name it accordingly. Practicing this step gives you a quick feedback loop: create the file, confirm service status, fix ownership and contexts, then test. How would you verify the content from another machine? Default Document Root and index.html means place an index.html in /var/www/html, set correct permissions and selinux context, then test with a browser or curl.. In practical terms, place web content in /var/www/html and verify access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Place an index.html in /var/www/html, set correct permissions and SELinux context, then test with a browser or curl.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Document Root
Default document root: /var/www/html
Create and serve a test page to confirm functionality.
<echo "<h1>Welcome to my Cohortia RHEL Web Server!</h1>" | sudo tee /var/www/html/index.html>
<sudo chmod -R 755 /var/www/html>
<sudo chown -R apache:apache /var/www/html>
<sudo restorecon -Rv /var/www/html>
<curl http://localhost/>
Common mistakes and fixes
  • Permission denied responses often mean wrong ownership or mode; set apache:apache and 755 recursively.
  • HTTP 403 can be caused by incorrect SELinux contexts; restorecon -Rv repairs labels to the expected type.
  • Assuming the firewall is at fault too early wastes time; verify service and file access locally first.
Analogy
Think of /var/www/html as a storefront window. If the light is off (service down) or the window is locked (permissions/SELinux), customers cannot see your page even if you opened the street (firewall).
Key Takeaway

Test locally first. Correct ownership and SELinux contexts are frequent causes of files not being served.

screens.title: Open HTTP/HTTPS in firewalld
screens.narratorSegment: A running web server is only reachable if the firewall permits the traffic. On RHEL, firewalld manages ingress rules and provides service names that map to ports. To allow HTTP and HTTPS in the public zone run: sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=http --permanent and sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=https --permanent, then reload the rules with sudo firewall-cmd --reload. The permanent flag writes the rule to the configuration so it persists after reboot; without it the port opens only until the next reload or reboot. After reloading, verify with sudo firewall-cmd --list-services --zone=public to see http and https listed. A frequent misconception is that reloading the firewall is optional; forgetting reload means the new permanent rules won’t take effect immediately and you will still be blocked. Another pitfall is adding ports rather than services; using service names is less error-prone because firewalld maps the right TCP or UDP ports automatically. Practice adding service rules and verifying them; if a connection still times out, re-check systemctl status, SELinux, and whether a network ACL is blocking traffic before assuming the service is misconfigured. Open HTTP/HTTPS in firewalld means add http and https services to the public zone permanently, reload firewalld, and verify the service list to ensure reachability.. In practical terms, allow web traffic through the default public zone. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Firewall steps
keyIdea.text: Add http and https services to the public zone permanently, reload firewalld, and verify the service list to ensure reachability.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Open Firewall
Commands to open web traffic
sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=http --permanent
sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=https --permanent
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
sudo firewall-cmd --list-services --zone=public
Use service names so firewalld opens the right ports for TCP or UDP automatically. Always reload after adding permanent rules.
Checks and troubleshooting
  • If connection still times out, confirm httpd is active with systemctl status httpd.
  • Verify SELinux context and file permissions if you get HTTP 403 errors instead of timeouts.
  • Use curl from another machine or telnet to port 80 to test reachability; timeouts usually indicate a firewall or network ACL issue.
Remember: forgetting to reload firewalld after adding permanent rules is the most common operational mistake here.
Key Takeaway

Open services with permanent rules and reload; verify with --list-services to avoid surprises.

screens.title: SELinux Contexts for Web Files
screens.narratorSegment: SELinux applies security labels known as contexts to files, processes, and ports. Apache will only serve files with the correct file context that allow the httpd process to read them. When you create web content manually, the files might inherit a context that prevents access. The command sudo restorecon -Rv /var/www/html restores the default contexts for the standard document root recursively. This command is safe: it resets labels to the distribution's expected values so services that depend on those labels work correctly. A common misconception is to change file permissions broadly to work around access denied errors. While permissions matter, incorrect SELinux labels often manifest as failures even when owner and mode look correct. In practice, run restorecon when Apache cannot read files, and avoid disabling SELinux as a shortcut. An example: you create index. html and chmod 644, but Apache returns a forbidden error. restorecon -Rv will likely resolve the issue. Always combine context fixes with proper ownership, and then test again. What would you do if restorecon does not clear the error? SELinux Contexts for Web Files means use restorecon to reset file contexts so httpd can access and serve content; don't disable selinux as a shortcut.. In practical terms, why restorecon matters and how to fix file-label problems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use restorecon to reset file contexts so httpd can access and serve content; don't disable SELinux as a shortcut.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › SELinux Contexts
Restore SELinux contexts for web files
Use restorecon to align file labels with service expectations.
sudo restorecon -Rv /var/www/html
# Verify label type with
ls -Z /var/www/html
If labels already look correct but access fails, review httpd logs and consider SELinux boolean settings for httpd if needed for advanced features; avoid turning SELinux off in production.
Explanation and example
  • SELinux contexts act as an additional access control layer beyond file ownership and permissions.
  • restorecon resets labels to the default types for the distribution, which is usually what httpd expects.
  • Listing files with ls -Z shows the SELinux type; look for httpd_sys_content_t or the expected web content type.
Misconception: Changing file permissions broadly may expose other services. Fix labels first and apply least-privilege permissions.
Key Takeaway

SELinux labels are the correct fix for many 'forbidden' errors; restorecon -Rv is a safe first step.

screens.title: Install and Start MariaDB Server
screens.narratorSegment: MariaDB provides the relational database backend many web applications require. Install it using sudo dnf install -y mariadb-server. After installation, enable and start the service with sudo systemctl enable --now mariadb and verify the unit with sudo systemctl status mariadb. Start by confirming the service is active then perform a local login attempt. A common mistake is skipping mysql_secure_installation and leaving default accounts or empty passwords; that will make your database vulnerable. Before you secure it, verify you can reach the local MariaDB prompt with mysql -u root -p; initially it may not accept a password if none is set. The next lesson covers using the mysql_secure_installation helper. If the service fails to start, review journalctl -u mariadb for error messages and ensure no conflicting configurations were added. Practice bringing the service up, checking status, and opening a local shell to confirm you can connect. After this, proceed to hardening so the server isn't left with default accounts and public access. Install and Start MariaDB Server means install mariadb-server, enable and start the mariadb service, and verify you can connect locally before proceeding to hardening.. In practical terms, set up mariadb-server and verify the service. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: MariaDB install
keyIdea.text: Install mariadb-server, enable and start the mariadb service, and verify you can connect locally before proceeding to hardening.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Install MariaDB
Install and verify MariaDB server
sudo dnf install -y mariadb-server
sudo systemctl enable --now mariadb
sudo systemctl status mariadb
# Test local login
mysql -u root -p
Confirm that mariadb accepts local connections before running the secure installation helper. If you cannot connect, check mariadb logs and unit status.
Practical guidance
  • Install the package so systemctl can manage the service unit and default configuration files are placed.
  • Enable and start the service to create runtime directories and socket files that some configurations expect.
  • Test login locally; many systems disallow remote root by default and require a secured root password.
Misconception: Installing mariadb-server implies secure defaults. Always run the secure installation helper to remove insecure defaults and set a root password.
Key Takeaway

Install and enable mariadb, then verify a local connection before hardening the server with mysql_secure_installation.

screens.title: Securing MariaDB with mysql_secure_installation
screens.narratorSegment: After installing and starting MariaDB you should immediately run sudo mysql_secure_installation. This interactive tool walks you through critical hardening steps: setting a strong root password, removing anonymous users, disabling remote root login, removing the test database, and reloading privilege tables. These steps remove common default weaknesses in fresh installations. For example, leaving the root account without a password or allowing anonymous users can let attackers access and manipulate your databases. During the interactive prompts, answer yes to remove anonymous users and the test database, and yes to reload the privilege tables. For remote root login the recommended response is no, preventing root from authenticating remotely. After completing the script, verify local root login with mysql -u root -p and the password you set. A common misconception is to postpone this script until later; delaying leaves the server exposed. Always harden immediately after installation and before placing production data or opening remote access. What principle connects these steps to secure administration? The answer is least privilege: remove anything not required for operation. Securing MariaDB with mysql_secure_installation means mysql_secure_installation guides you to set root password, remove anonymous users, disallow remote root login, and remove test databases.. In practical terms, hardening defaults: set root password and remove unsafe users. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Secure MariaDB
Run the interactive hardening script
Follow the prompts and apply recommended answers for production systems.
sudo mysql_secure_installation
# Typical prompts and recommended answers:
# - Set root password? (Y)
# - Remove anonymous users? (Y)
# - Disallow root login remotely? (Y)
# - Remove test database? (Y)
# - Reload privilege tables? (Y)
Why each step matters
  • Setting a root password prevents unauthenticated access to the database server.
  • Removing anonymous users ensures only named accounts can authenticate.
  • Disallowing remote root logins forces use of less-privileged accounts for remote work.
  • Removing the test database closes a common backdoor used during initial installs.
Misconception: skipping these steps because it's 'just a lab' creates unsafe habits. Treat each fresh install as if it will go into production.
Key Takeaway

Hardening with mysql_secure_installation is quick and addresses the most common initial vulnerabilities.

screens.title: Common Troubleshooting: Web vs Database Issues
screens.narratorSegment: When a service seems unreachable you must determine whether the issue lies with the service itself, the firewall, or SELinux. For a web server that times out, start by checking systemctl status httpd. If the service is not active, troubleshoot logs with journalctl -u httpd. If the service is active but the connection times out from a remote machine, test curl or telnet locally on the server. If local curl works but remote does not, the firewall is the likely culprit — verify firewalld rules with firewall-cmd --list-services --zone=public and ensure http/https are present and that reload was performed. If you see HTTP 403 forbidden errors instead, file permissions or SELinux contexts are common causes. For MariaDB, local connection failures suggest service or authentication issues; use journalctl -u mariadb and attempt mysql -u root -p locally. If you cannot log in because of missing root password, run mysql_secure_installation. A common misunderstanding is to change multiple settings at once; make one change and re-test. This structured approach—service check, local test, firewall, SELinux—reduces time spent chasing the wrong layer. Which check will you run first next time you face a timeout?

keyIdea.text: Check service status, test locally, then inspect firewall rules and SELinux contexts. Change one thing at a time and retest.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Troubleshooting
Web server timeout vs forbidden
Follow a checklist to isolate the layer causing the problem.
# Service check
sudo systemctl status httpd
# Local test
curl http://localhost/
# Firewall check
sudo firewall-cmd --list-services --zone=public
# SELinux fix
sudo restorecon -Rv /var/www/html
Database connection issues
Check service, local login, and secure installation.
sudo systemctl status mariadb
sudo journalctl -u mariadb
mysql -u root -p
sudo mysql_secure_installation
Pro tip

Change one thing at a time and retest. This isolates cause and prevents cascading misconfigurations.

screens.title: Basic Service Architecture on a Single Host
screens.narratorSegment: On many RHEL hosts Apache and MariaDB run side-by-side: Apache serves HTTP(S) requests and forwards application data or dynamic queries to MariaDB which stores structured data. They use separate ports and separate service units; httpd listens on ports 80 and 443 while MariaDB listens on its native port for local or remote clients. Keep database listeners bound to localhost unless remote access is required and secured. On a single host, the OS controls access via systemctl, firewalld, and SELinux; each plays a role. Systemctl manages process lifecycle, firewalld manages network reachability, and SELinux controls cross-process file and resource access at a finer level. Practically, you install both services, run httpd to serve pages from /var/www/html, and run MariaDB with a secure root password and least-privilege database accounts for application users. A misconception is that both services require the same level of openness — databases should be more restricted. The architecture decision to bind MariaDB to localhost by default reduces attack surface and enforces the principle of least privilege. Consider whether your web application needs a remote database or if local sockets suffice; often local access is both faster and safer.

keyIdea.text: Apache and MariaDB commonly run on one host but should be separated by network and privilege controls: web facing vs restricted database access.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Service Architecture
Single-host architecture overview
Typical flow: client → Apache → application → MariaDB (local).
Apache HTTPD
Listens on 80/443, serves files from /var/www/html and passes dynamic requests to backend components.
MariaDB
Provides relational storage. Secure default: harden root account and prefer local connections.
Controls
systemctl for lifecycle, firewalld for network exposure, SELinux for fine-grained resource access control.
Practical guidance
  • Keep database listeners local unless necessary; use firewalld to restrict access otherwise.
  • Create application database users with only the privileges needed for their tasks.
  • Regularly update packages to patch service vulnerabilities.
Key Takeaway

Segregate access: web-facing components need broader network exposure than database services, which should follow least privilege.

screens.title: Hands-on Activity Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Follow this step-by-step sequence in the lab to complete the hands-on activity from the chapter. Start by installing Apache with sudo dnf install -y httpd. Then enable and start the service using sudo systemctl enable --now httpd and confirm it is active. Create a simple web page by echoing H T M L into /var/www/html/index. html, then set ownership and permissions with sudo chown -R apache:apache /var/www/html and sudo chmod -R 755 /var/www/html. If Apache cannot read the files, run sudo restorecon -Rv /var/www/html to fix SELinux contexts. Next, open HTTP and HTTPS in the firewall: add the services permanently with sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=http --permanent and sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=https --permanent, then reload with sudo firewall-cmd --reload. Verify the site from a browser or curl. For MariaDB, install with sudo dnf install -y mariadb-server, enable and start it with sudo systemctl enable --now mariadb, and immediately run sudo mysql_secure_installation to harden the installation. Finish by testing local login with mysql -u root -p to confirm your root password works. If any step fails, use the troubleshooting checklist from earlier: service status, local test, firewall, SELinux. Which step gave you the clearest feedback in your run?

Install and enable Apache

screens.title: Assessment & Common Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Let's reinforce your understanding with an assessment idea from the chapter and a review of common mistakes. A diagnostic question asks: after installing Apache and creating index. html, remote access times out. Which is the most likely reason? The correct diagnosis is that the firewall blocks HTTP traffic and the fix is to add the http service in firewalld and reload. This reveals a common operational mistake: checking the wrong layer first. Another common error is forgetting to run mysql_secure_installation after installing MariaDB, which leaves default accounts and weak or empty root passwords. Administrators also sometimes change permissions excessively to fix access problems; this weakens security. Practice the lab steps in order and adopt a habit of checking service status, testing locally, then verifying firewall and SELinux. For the quiz, try to answer: what is the default document root for Apache on RHEL, and why must you run restorecon when files are manually created? The answers are /var/www/html and restorecon corrects SELinux labels so httpd can access files. How would you explain least privilege when creating database users? Assessment & Common Mistakes means check service status, firewall, and selinux in that order. run mysql_secure_installation immediately and avoid overbroad permission changes.. In practical terms, quick quiz and mistakes to avoid when deploying services. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Quiz item
Q: Default web root on RHEL? A: /var/www/html
Q: Primary fix for Apache file-label problems? A: restorecon -Rv /var/www/html
Common mistakes

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will study the essential steps to get a web server and a database server running and reachable on a RHEL system. We'll cover installing Apache HTTPD and MariaDB using the dnf package manager, starting and enabling services with systemctl, and the basic security steps that make these services safe to expose. You will see concrete commands to create a simple web page under the default document root, adjust SELinux contexts and file permissions when Apache cannot read files, and open HTTP and HTTPS through firewalld so external clients can reach your server. For MariaDB, we'll install the server package, start the service, and run the interactive mysql_secure_installation script to set a root password and remove insecure defaults. These are foundational operations you will run often as an RHCSA. A common pitfall is thinking a service is unreachable because it failed to start, when in practice the firewall or SELinux labels are blocking access. By the end of this chapter you will be able to install both services, verify they run, fix basic access problems, and perform the initial hardening steps that reduce risk. Consider how least privilege and routine updates fit into daily administration — that mindset makes these steps meaningful beyond the commands.

These four objectives focus your practice on the essential operations for web and database services on RHEL. First, you will install and perform initial configuration of Apache HTTPD so a static site can be served. This includes using the package manager, creating an index page in the default web root, and checking that the httpd service runs. Second, you will manage the httpd service lifecycle with systemctl and configure firewalld to permit HTTP and HTTPS traffic so remote clients can reach the server. A concrete example is opening the public zone for the http service and reloading the firewall to apply the change. Third, you will install MariaDB, start and enable the service, and run the mysql_secure_installation script to set a strong root password and remove insecure defaults. Fourth, you will learn the early steps to secure common network services: correct SELinux file contexts, file permissions, and the principle of least privilege when creating database accounts. Each objective is practical and directly applicable during labs and in production. Practice these steps in order, because a running service that is blocked by the firewall or mis-labeled by SELinux will appear broken even when correctly installed. Which objective will you try first in your lab?

This page outlines a recommended sequence so your lab runs without surprises. Start by installing packages with dnf so the binaries and unit files exist. Then enable and start services to ensure systemctl-created sockets and directories are present; this avoids file-permission anomalies later. Next, create a minimal index file in the default document root and adjust SELinux contexts and ownership so Apache can read it. Only after the service runs and file access is confirmed should you change firewall rules to expose the service. For MariaDB, install and start the service, then immediately run mysql_secure_installation to remove anonymous users and set root password. Test the database locally before permitting remote access. Following this order reduces troubleshooting complexity: if you open firewall ports before verifying service availability, you may think the firewall is the problem when the service itself is down or misconfigured. Practice the sequence in the lab to build muscle memory. The lab activity included in the chapter follows this flow step-by-step and ends with a verification step: browse to http://your_rhel_server_ip and log into MariaDB locally. Which step would you try twice to gain confidence?

To install Apache HTTPD on RHEL you use the distribution package manager so the httpd binary, unit files, and configuration skeleton are all placed correctly. The canonical command is sudo dnf install -y httpd. Running this fetches the httpd package and any required dependencies. After installation, systemctl knows about the httpd unit and you can enable and start it with sudo systemctl enable --now httpd. Enabling with --now both starts the service immediately and ensures it will start on boot. Verify the unit with sudo systemctl status httpd which reports whether the service is active and any recent errors. A concrete example: in the lab you might install httpd, enable the service, then check status and see it active. If status shows a failure, examine the journal with sudo journalctl -u httpd. A common misconception is that package installation alone makes the site reachable; you must start and enable the service. Also avoid assuming the default document root contains your custom content — create an index page explicitly. Practice these commands until you can reliably install, start, and check httpd. What would you check first if systemctl status shows the service failed?

Apache serves files from a document root. On RHEL the default is /var/www/html. Creating a simple index. html file there is the fastest way to verify the server serves content. For example, echo "<h1>Welcome to my Cohortia RHEL Web Server!</h1>" | sudo tee /var/www/html/index. html writes a test page. After placing the file, ensure the httpd service is running and then browse to the server IP or curl the address locally. A common mistake is assuming the file is readable—permissions or SELinux contexts may prevent Apache from serving it. Use sudo chmod -R 755 /var/www/html and sudo chown -R apache:apache /var/www/html to set ownership and basic permissions. If SELinux prevents access, restore contexts with sudo restorecon -Rv /var/www/html. Another misconception is that the index filename can be arbitrary; by default Apache looks for index. html among other welcome files, so name it accordingly. Practicing this step gives you a quick feedback loop: create the file, confirm service status, fix ownership and contexts, then test. How would you verify the content from another machine? Default Document Root and index.html means place an index.html in /var/www/html, set correct permissions and selinux context, then test with a browser or curl.. In practical terms, place web content in /var/www/html and verify access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A running web server is only reachable if the firewall permits the traffic. On RHEL, firewalld manages ingress rules and provides service names that map to ports. To allow HTTP and HTTPS in the public zone run: sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=http --permanent and sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=https --permanent, then reload the rules with sudo firewall-cmd --reload. The permanent flag writes the rule to the configuration so it persists after reboot; without it the port opens only until the next reload or reboot. After reloading, verify with sudo firewall-cmd --list-services --zone=public to see http and https listed. A frequent misconception is that reloading the firewall is optional; forgetting reload means the new permanent rules won’t take effect immediately and you will still be blocked. Another pitfall is adding ports rather than services; using service names is less error-prone because firewalld maps the right TCP or UDP ports automatically. Practice adding service rules and verifying them; if a connection still times out, re-check systemctl status, SELinux, and whether a network ACL is blocking traffic before assuming the service is misconfigured. Open HTTP/HTTPS in firewalld means add http and https services to the public zone permanently, reload firewalld, and verify the service list to ensure reachability.. In practical terms, allow web traffic through the default public zone. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

SELinux applies security labels known as contexts to files, processes, and ports. Apache will only serve files with the correct file context that allow the httpd process to read them. When you create web content manually, the files might inherit a context that prevents access. The command sudo restorecon -Rv /var/www/html restores the default contexts for the standard document root recursively. This command is safe: it resets labels to the distribution's expected values so services that depend on those labels work correctly. A common misconception is to change file permissions broadly to work around access denied errors. While permissions matter, incorrect SELinux labels often manifest as failures even when owner and mode look correct. In practice, run restorecon when Apache cannot read files, and avoid disabling SELinux as a shortcut. An example: you create index. html and chmod 644, but Apache returns a forbidden error. restorecon -Rv will likely resolve the issue. Always combine context fixes with proper ownership, and then test again. What would you do if restorecon does not clear the error? MariaDB provides the relational database backend many web applications require. Install it using sudo dnf install -y mariadb-server. After installation, enable and start the service with sudo systemctl enable --now mariadb and verify the unit with sudo systemctl status mariadb. Start by confirming the service is active then perform a local login attempt. A common mistake is skipping mysql_secure_installation and leaving default accounts or empty passwords; that will make your database vulnerable. Before you secure it, verify you can reach the local MariaDB prompt with mysql -u root -p; initially it may not accept a password if none is set. The next lesson covers using the mysql_secure_installation helper. If the service fails to start, review journalctl -u mariadb for error messages and ensure no conflicting configurations were added. Practice bringing the service up, checking status, and opening a local shell to confirm you can connect. After this, proceed to hardening so the server isn't left with default accounts and public access. After installing and starting MariaDB you should immediately run sudo mysql_secure_installation. This interactive tool walks you through critical hardening steps: setting a strong root password, removing anonymous users, disabling remote root login, removing the test database, and reloading privilege tables. These steps remove common default weaknesses in fresh installations. For example, leaving the root account without a password or allowing anonymous users can let attackers access and manipulate your databases. During the interactive prompts, answer yes to remove anonymous users and the test database, and yes to reload the privilege tables. For remote root login the recommended response is no, preventing root from authenticating remotely. After completing the script, verify local root login with mysql -u root -p and the password you set. A common misconception is to postpone this script until later; delaying leaves the server exposed. Always harden immediately after installation and before placing production data or opening remote access. What principle connects these steps to secure administration? The answer is least privilege: remove anything not required for operation. In practical terms, hardening defaults: set root password and remove unsafe users. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. When a service seems unreachable you must determine whether the issue lies with the service itself, the firewall, or SELinux. For a web server that times out, start by checking systemctl status httpd. If the service is not active, troubleshoot logs with journalctl -u httpd. If the service is active but the connection times out from a remote machine, test curl or telnet locally on the server. If local curl works but remote does not, the firewall is the likely culprit — verify firewalld rules with firewall-cmd --list-services --zone=public and ensure http/https are present and that reload was performed. If you see HTTP 403 forbidden errors instead, file permissions or SELinux contexts are common causes. For MariaDB, local connection failures suggest service or authentication issues; use journalctl -u mariadb and attempt mysql -u root -p locally. If you cannot log in because of missing root password, run mysql_secure_installation. A common misunderstanding is to change multiple settings at once; make one change and re-test. This structured approach—service check, local test, firewall, SELinux—reduces time spent chasing the wrong layer. Which check will you run first next time you face a timeout?

On many RHEL hosts Apache and MariaDB run side-by-side: Apache serves HTTP(S) requests and forwards application data or dynamic queries to MariaDB which stores structured data. They use separate ports and separate service units; httpd listens on ports 80 and 443 while MariaDB listens on its native port for local or remote clients. Keep database listeners bound to localhost unless remote access is required and secured. On a single host, the OS controls access via systemctl, firewalld, and SELinux; each plays a role. Systemctl manages process lifecycle, firewalld manages network reachability, and SELinux controls cross-process file and resource access at a finer level. Practically, you install both services, run httpd to serve pages from /var/www/html, and run MariaDB with a secure root password and least-privilege database accounts for application users. A misconception is that both services require the same level of openness — databases should be more restricted. The architecture decision to bind MariaDB to localhost by default reduces attack surface and enforces the principle of least privilege. Consider whether your web application needs a remote database or if local sockets suffice; often local access is both faster and safer.

Follow this step-by-step sequence in the lab to complete the hands-on activity from the chapter. Start by installing Apache with sudo dnf install -y httpd. Then enable and start the service using sudo systemctl enable --now httpd and confirm it is active. Create a simple web page by echoing H T M L into /var/www/html/index. html, then set ownership and permissions with sudo chown -R apache:apache /var/www/html and sudo chmod -R 755 /var/www/html. If Apache cannot read the files, run sudo restorecon -Rv /var/www/html to fix SELinux contexts. Next, open HTTP and HTTPS in the firewall: add the services permanently with sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=http --permanent and sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=https --permanent, then reload with sudo firewall-cmd --reload. Verify the site from a browser or curl. For MariaDB, install with sudo dnf install -y mariadb-server, enable and start it with sudo systemctl enable --now mariadb, and immediately run sudo mysql_secure_installation to harden the installation. Finish by testing local login with mysql -u root -p to confirm your root password works. If any step fails, use the troubleshooting checklist from earlier: service status, local test, firewall, SELinux. Which step gave you the clearest feedback in your run?
